$comment: Every UI surface a config/integration-manifest.json entry or a config/settings-keys.json entry may name, and whether it exists. `built` is mechanical: tools/integration-audit/verify-parity.mjs requires the named component to exist and to render data-surface="<surfaceId>". The per-entry `reachable` in each of those two files is the claim that a user can actually reach that thing through the surface, and it may only be true where the surface is built. The two are separate because a surface can exist and still not configure everything it lists -- see Settings > Transcription below. tools/settings-audit/scan.mjs goes one step further for a settings key: the surface's component must call the IPC wrapper for the command that writes that key, so naming a screen is not enough.

Settings > Providers.note: Stores a key for every one of the seventeen provider and custom-endpoint credential slots the registry declares -- the three enterprise slots are multi-field and configured on Settings > Intelligence > Enterprise instead -- and runs the real connection test. Write-only: no command returns a credential value, so the field replaces or removes and never displays. A stored key is reported as stored, never as connected.

Settings > Transcription.note: Chooses the cloud provider and model for dictation, from the registry. Six of the seven providers can be selected: three over HttpBatch and three through their own client in crates/transcription-core/src/clients.rs. Corti also takes an environment and a tenant here, because the router refuses to guess either. Tinfoil is listed with the reason it is refused -- an unattested request would present as Tinfoil while providing none of what the name means. Keys are stored on Settings > Providers.

Settings > Transcription > Local.note: Offers the six whisper models and, since 121dc4c, the two Parakeet models through the sherpa-onnx sidecar -- sherpa_install_model installs the CLI too if it is missing, and sherpa_use_model resolves a selection before remembering it, so a model that cannot run is refused now rather than at the next dictation. One local engine, not two: a selected sherpa model wins over a running whisper server, and local_server_start clears the sherpa selection. The two Nemotron entries stay unreachable for an unrelated reason -- they are streaming models over sherpa's own WebSocket protocol, which nobody has built a client for. Writes transcription.localModel and transcription.sherpaModel (config/settings-keys.json).

Settings > Intelligence.note: Configures the reasoning provider and model that tidy a dictation, and switches cleanup on. The three enterprise connectors and the local route are listed with the reason they cannot be used, rather than being left out -- so this surface is built while Settings > Intelligence > Enterprise and > Local are not.

Settings > Intelligence > Local.note: Installs and runs the pinned llama.cpp CPU build and any of the registry's GGUF models. Sizes are shown before the install button because the recommended model is 5.9 GB, and the five-minute idle shutdown is stated rather than being a surprise later.

Settings > Intelligence > Enterprise.note: A form per connector on the Intelligence screen. The request signing and body shapes are written and tested against AWS's published SigV4 vectors and recorded fixtures; no live call has been made, and the section says so on screen as well as in PLATFORM_SUPPORT.md.

Settings > Meetings.note: Shared recognition hints are managed in Vocabulary. Sets the meeting provider, the prompt-on-detect switch, the language hint, and the allow and deny lists deciding which applications count as a meeting. The lists were the fourth capability found honoured by the backend with no way in, and the first found by tools/settings-audit/scan.mjs rather than by a person reading a screen (KNEG-114); they are edited under the list of running applications, because the name to type is the one each detection there reports. Since KNEG-334 this is the settings page only, filed under Settings in the rail: the recording task moved to the Meetings surface below, and this screen also resets the notification window's placement and switches speaker labels on. The provider is saved on change and the language when its field is left or Enter is pressed, because Start is on the Meetings page now: Rust reads the language from the database when a meeting starts, and the provider is the one the Meetings page reads back from meetings.provider and passes to meeting_start. Both fields are disabled while a meeting is live.

Meetings.note: The recording task: whether a meeting can be recorded (lib/readiness.ts), Start/Stop/Discard, whether the other participants are captured, the live transcript and interrupted recordings. The provider and language are chosen here, in the control bar chips, and also set on Settings > Meetings, which owns them along with detection. The microphone chip names the one chosen on Dictation (audio.inputDevice, shared by both tasks), or says it is not connected and the default will be recorded; it is shown here, not chosen. A local provider that cannot start (no model installed, no streaming model chosen or downloaded) holds Start with a fix to Settings > Transcription; Start itself brings the local Whisper server up when it is not running.

Settings > Shortcuts.note: Binds an accelerator to each of the five hotkey actions and writes hotkey.<action>, and since 2026-09-01 (KNEG-64) picks toggle or hold-to-talk per action and writes hotkey.<action>.mode. Moved here from the Dictation page (KNEG-334), and the evidence moved with it: Last fired and Last dictation result sit under the editor, so binding a key and seeing whether anything handled it are still on one screen -- the first bench check could not tell "the hotkey did nothing" from "the hotkey saved nothing". The Dictation page shows the last result as well and links here to change its shortcut. The accelerator field also takes Mouse4 and Mouse5, which go to the WH_MOUSE_LL hook; the mode selector ships as toggle for every action and the screen says why holding is offered rather than defaulted. Four of the five actions have no handler; commands::hotkeys reports that as an UnhandledAction rather than letting a bound key look wired.

Dictation.note: The dictation task: whether it will work (lib/readiness.ts) and the shortcut to press, in a centred hero; then a control bar with the microphone, the route (an installed model on this computer or a cloud provider) and, on the local whisper route, the languages, each chosen in place in its chip's menu -- the route and the languages only between dictations, since Rust reads them at Stop, and they are also set on Settings > Transcription, which owns them; a Tidy up chip that switches cleanup on and off once it has been set up in Settings > Cleanup & summaries (held during a dictation, and saying under itself when it cannot run), and until then links there; the privacy line; the last result; and the Start button, held while a route switch is applied. The shortcut editor is on Settings > Shortcuts, reached from the history panel.

Dictation > History.note: Dictation's list panel: the history grouped by day, and under History options the switches that turn history off and keep the pre-cleanup transcript, and Clear history. The first two controls exist because the backend honoured history.enabled and history.keepRawText with no way in (KNEG-98, KNEG-99) -- the pattern tools/settings-audit/scan.mjs now gates. Moved out of views/Dictation.tsx into the panel in KNEG-363.

Integrations > Calendar.note: Google and Microsoft: register your own OAuth client and paste the client ID in on this screen, then connect and sync -- the screen says why there is no embedded client. Apple shows kw_calendar_core::apple::support()'s reason rather than an empty calendar list.

Integrations > CLI.note: Shows the compiled knegiswhisper binary's location (a real check next to this running application and on PATH, never assumed), the discovery file's path, and the discovery file's real permission state as a tagged union with evidence -- ten states, each with its own sentence in discoveryPermissionsLabel, rather than the boolean is_as_expected() would collapse them to. That boolean has been deleted; DiscoveryPermissions::is_confirmed() draws the line at checked versus unchecked, so owner-and-administrators passes (the access list was read back) and inherited-from-profile does not (nothing looked). See docs/BENCH_CHECK.md, 2026-08-26 finding 2.

Integrations > MCP.note: Shows the exact stdio command line for tools/knegiswhisper-mcp (binary path plus empty args) to paste into an MCP client's config, and states plainly that the local API must be running -- the server has no backend of its own. The binary's presence is a real check next to this running application and on PATH, never assumed.

Notes > Upload.note: Audio and video import (Task 11's media.rs, driving the ffmpeg sidecar pinned in config/sidecars.json), plus the OpenWhispr database importer (storage::import::from_openwhispr), which existed and was tested since early in the build but had no screen until now. URL import was withdrawn -- media_import_url is unregistered as a command, this screen offers no URL field, and media:url-import is reachable: false; the yt-dlp sidecar stays pinned for a re-opening that has not happened. The screen renders the full ImportReport -- what copied, what was dropped per table, and which credentials moved into the OS credential store -- not just a success message. Every path this screen imports must be one pick_import_file returned: commands::DialogGrants records the canonical form of each dialog-returned path and media_import_audio, media_import_video and import_openwhispr refuse anything else, so a path this screen invented rather than picked is refused before the file is opened (docs/SECURITY.md, Webview).

Vocabulary.note: Shared dictionary management and provider-specific recognition-hint usage. Legacy meeting keyterms are migrated into dictionary storage.

Settings > Intelligence > Summaries.note: Configures automatic summaries independently of dictation cleanup, including destination, language and context budget.
